newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gore underlines U.S. security commitment in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Gore underlines U.S. security commitment in Asia.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore, beginning a trip designed to improve relations with China, on Sunday ruled out any cuts in U.S. forces in Japan, saying it was the "worst time" for such reductions.

Although the primary focus of the trip is the four days Gore spends in China, his Sunday night talks with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda underscored a lingering problem Washington faces in Japan -- the controversy over the size of its military contingent here.
As he posed for pictures with Ikeda, Gore was asked if the current force can be reduced over the next decade. "I think we need them now and for the foreseeable future," he replied.
"In my view, this would be the worst time to have some reduction in U.S. forces here," Gore said. "The current level is the appropriate level."

"The Japanese government feels that the U.S. military is an important factor for stability in the region," Japanese Foreign Ministry officials quoted Ikeda as telling Gore. "Now is not the time to start discussions on reducing U.S. troops."
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, an action Tokyo strongly opposes.
Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he planned to push through parliament a new law to seek continued leases on private land used by U.S. bases on Okinawa.
On Monday, Gore meets Hashimoto, delivers a speech on the environment and visits a U.S. air base before departing for Beijing and talks the next day with President Jiang Zemin.
"This visit is intended to reaffirm once again America's commitment to the region overall," Gore said during an arrival ceremony held in steady rain.
"The security and prosperity of the United States is vitally tied to the Asia-Pacific region," Gore said.

Chatting with reporters aboard Air Force Two, Gore sounded upbeat about the chances for improving relations with China, which has frequently clashed with Washington in recent years, particularly over trade, Taiwan and human rights.
"Change is taking place rapidly inside China ... the growth of the free sector of their economy is far outstripping the growth in the state-owned sector," he said.

"Both our countries are clearly signalling to one another that we want to find a way to move forward in the relationship," said Gore, who planned to discuss a broad range of issues including the environment and the future of Hong Kong.

"I hope to have meaningful discussions in China," said Gore, adding that he would "touch on every issue that has a particular impact for our two countries" -- including charges Beijing tried to funnel money to influence last year's presidential elections and some congressional races.
Gore will be the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush in 1989 -- shortly before Chinese troops brutally ended pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.

At least part of his discussions will deal with preparations for an exchange of visits by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Jiang. The Chinese leader is expected to visit the United States late this year and Clinton tentatively plans to go to China in 1998.

Gore said that high on his agenda was a discussion about possible four-way talks between the two Koreas and the United States and China, an idea that was proposed in April by Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
The four-way talks would be designed to bring a formal end to the 1950-1953 Korean War.
